profile.summary: VESPAl is the light version of VESPA, a predictor of the effect of single amino acid substitutions in a protein. It needs only the protein sequence: no alignment and no structure. It embeds the sequence with the ProtT5 protein language model, predicts how conserved each residue is, and then scores each substitution with a logistic regression ensemble that takes that conservation prediction together with BLOSUM62 substitution scores. Unlike full VESPA it leaves out the language model substitution probabilities, which the authors say costs a small drop in accuracy and makes whole proteomes affordable.

summary_quotes.text: **VESPA** is a simple, yet powerful Single Amino Acid Variant (SAV) effect predictor based on embeddings of the Protein Language Model
by using the computationally more efficient method VESPA-light (**VESPAl**) with only step (2) as input for a small drop in prediction performance
by excluding substitution probabilities to allow proteome-wide analysis to complete after the coffee break on a single machine

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: VESPAl is the light version of VESPA. It keeps the first two steps of the pipeline, embedding the sequence with ProtT5 and predicting per-residue conservation in nine classes, and then scores a variant from that conservation prediction together with BLOSUM62 substitution scores. It leaves out the third step, the per-variant log-odds ratios of masked marginal probabilities, which is the step that needs a GPU. The scorer is the same kind of balanced logistic regression ensemble as VESPA, trained on rotated cross-validation splits of the Eff10k set of binary variant effect annotations, and the repository ships it as a separate model file, VESPAl-10LR_Cons_Blsm.pkl, next to VESPA's VESPA-10LR_Cons_Blsm_Prob.pkl.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one released version of the software rather than a family of checkpoints: pyproject.toml gives the package as vespa-effect version 1.0.2 at the commit read here, and the trained models ship inside the repository as three files, ProtT5cons_checkpoint.pt for the conservation predictor and one pickle each for VESPA and VESPAl. A result should name the package version or the commit, and the ProtT5 weights used for the embeddings, because those are downloaded separately at run time into the cache folder the command names. The README also offers an experimental install of the v0.9.0-beta release from GitHub.

sections.title: Precomputed predictions and services
sections.body: Some predictions are published rather than computed. The README points to precomputed VESPA and VESPAl predictions for 39 deep mutational scanning experiments in the paper's supplementary file 3, and to VESPAl predictions for the whole human proteome and for the fly proteome on Zenodo. The paper says the methods are also available through bioembeddings.com, the repository and PredictProtein.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Supervised variant effect predictor: a logistic regression ensemble on top of protein language model features, scoring single amino acid substitutions without alignments.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Two stages: a supervised nine-class conservation predictor over ProtT5 embeddings, then an ensemble of ten logistic regressions taking that conservation prediction and BLOSUM62 scores. The log-odds step that VESPA adds is left out.
facts.source_locator: README: header, Step 2 and Step 3; paper: Fig. 1 caption; models folder listing

quotes.text: with only step (2) as input for a small drop in prediction performance
Input embedding into supervised method (here: logistic regression, FNN or CNN) to predict conservation in 9-classes as defined by ConSurf-DB

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: One FASTA file of wild-type sequences, with any number of sequences, and optionally a mutations file listing protein ID and substitution per line. No alignment and no structure.

quotes.text: **Required**: A single `FASTA` file containing all your wildtype sequences (note: this file can contain any number of sequences).
A simple text file with a protein ID and one mutation per-line

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: One semicolon separated CSV file per protein with a row per substitution and the predicted effect score, optionally a single HDF5 file holding a 20 by L matrix per sequence. A map.json links the numbered CSV files to sequence IDs.

quotes.text: will generate one .csv (with semicolon separator) file per protein in the output folder
The file contains one 20xL-shaped matrix per sequence-ID.
A lookup file `map.json` will be created in the output directory containing a dictionary mapping from number to sequence ID.

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: Not reported as a count. The scorer is an ensemble of ten logistic regressions shipped as a pickle of about 5 kB, and the conservation predictor checkpoint is 3,708,479 bytes; the ProtT5 language model it uses is downloaded separately and is not part of this release.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: Eff10k for the effect scorer: 100,737 binary variant effect annotations from 9,594 proteins, taken from the SNAP2 development set. ConSurf10k for the conservation predictor: 10,507 proteins or domains split into 9,392 training, 555 validation and 519 test sequences. No deep mutational scanning data was used for fitting.

quotes.text: It contained 100,737 binary SAV-effect annotations (neutral: 39,700, effect: 61,037) from 9594 proteins.
with 10,507 proteins (or domains) was randomly partitioned into training (9392 sequences), cross-training/validation (555), and test (519) sets
predicted SAV effect magnitude without any optimization on DMS data

run_guide.summary: Install the pip package and score every possible single amino acid substitution in a FASTA file with VESPAl.
prerequisites: Python at least 3.8 and below 3.11, as pyproject.toml requires.
A GPU for the embedding step: the README recommends at least 12 GB of VRAM. With precomputed embeddings the README says VESPAl needs no GPU.
A FASTA file of wild-type sequences, and optionally a mutations file.
Disk space for the ProtT5 weights, which are downloaded into the cache folder on first run.

steps.title: Install the package
steps.explanation: The install the README prefers. It brings the trained VESPAl model with it.

steps.title: Run VESPAl on a FASTA file
steps.explanation: The README quickstart. It runs VESPAl for all possible mutations by default, creating a vespa_run_directory with the input features and an output folder of CSV predictions. The cache folder keeps the ProtT5 weights between runs.

quotes.text: By default, this runs **VESPAl** for all possible mutations.

steps.title: Or run the substeps, reusing embeddings to avoid a GPU
steps.shell:
vespa_emb data/sequences.fasta -o data/embeddings.h5  --prott5_weights_cache data/cache
vespa_conspred data/embeddings.h5 -o data/conspred.h5
vespa_run data/conspred_probs.h5 data/sequences.fasta --output predictions/
steps.explanation: The three README substeps for VESPAl: embed, predict conservation, then score. The README says that with existing embeddings, passing use_existing_embeddings, VESPAl needs no GPU. Note that the README's embedding step writes conspred.h5 while its run step reads conspred_probs.h5, as printed.

quotes.text: you can use those instead of generating new ones by adding `--use_existing_embeddings` followed by the file location. Then running **VESPAl** will not require a GPU.

outputs: A vespa_run_directory, or the output directory given, holding one semicolon separated CSV per sequence with a row per substitution and its score, plus map.json linking file numbers to sequence IDs.
Optionally an HDF5 file with a 20 by L matrix per sequence, where fields that were not computed hold -1.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository README at commit 34fd1ab1b7fdc2b4e1a241fdae1db5c2f09d8944 and have not been executed by Rewire.
The README's substep file names are inconsistent between the conservation step and the run step; they are reproduced as printed.
The ProtT5 weights are downloaded at run time, so the exact language model revision used is not pinned by the sources.

notes: VESPAl and VESPA are two models from one repository and one paper, and this record covers the light one. The pair cannot be separated by source: the same pip package, README and commit serve both, and the records 13-vespa and 14-vespal should keep the same sources while differing in which pipeline steps and which model file they describe. The trained models are not released as separate weights: they ship inside the repository and the pip package, so the weights licence is the package licence, AGPL-3.0-or-later. No release date is stated, so structured.released is null. The input.json for this record lists the paper full text as an existing source, so no ProteinGym README was fetched here; the companion record 13-vespa carries that file.
